texts.preamble: The Food Inspector Rep., By The Pp vs Meda Bapu Reddy on 1 October, 2024 The Honourable Sri Justice K.Surender Criminal Appeal No.937 Of 2013 Judgment:
texts.facts: This criminal appeal is filed by appellant/food inspector aggrieved by the judgment, dated 09.10.2009 in C.C.No.316 of 2005 on the file of Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Chennur, wherein respondent/accused was acquitted for the offence under Section 7(i) 2(1a) (m) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 (for short "the Act"), which is punishable under Section 16(1) (a) (i) of the Act. Briefly, the case of the appellant/PW1/food inspector is that he went to the premises of shop run by the accused and found about 30 kgs of Bengal gram dal in gunny bag. Since the Bengal Gram was meant for public sale and there was suspicion that it was adulterated, PW1/food inspector purchased 1500 grams of Bengal gram dal from the above stock in cash under receipt/Ex.P2. After purchasing the same, PW1/food inspector divided the purchased Bengal KS,J crla_937_2013 gram dal into three parts weighing 500 grams of each sample. One of the samples was sent for the purpose of analysis by the public analyst. The public analyst sent the report opining that the sample does not confirm to the standards of Wevilled grains and therefore adulterated. 4. Having sent the notice to the accused along with the report and after obtaining permission, the complaint was filed. 5. Learned Magistrate examined PW1/food inspector and PW2 Panch witness. PW2 turned hostile to the prosecution case and did not support the version of PW1 that the Bengal gram dal was seized from the premises of the accused. 6. Learned Magistrate acquitted the accused on the following grounds: a) Panch witness PW2 did not support the case of the prosecution. KS,J crla_937_2013 d) None of the adjacent shop keepers to the accused shop were examined.
texts.arguments: The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Babu v. State of Kerala 1 held as follows: " 12. In State of Rajasthan v. Naresh @ Ram Naresh [(2009) 9 SCC 368], the Court again examined the earlier judgments of this Court and laid down that an "order of acquittal should not be lightly interfered with even if the court believes that there is some evidence pointing out the finger towards the accused." 13. In State of Uttar Pradesh v. Banne alias Baijnath & Ors. [(2009) 4 SCC 271], this Court gave certain illustrative circumstances in which the Court would be justified in interfering with a judgment of acquittal by the High Court. The circumstances includes: i) The High Court's decision is based on totally erroneous view of law by ignoring the settled legal position; ii) The High Court's conclusions are contrary to evidence and documents on record; Crl.A.No.104/09, dated 11.08.2010 KS,J crla_937_2013 iii) The entire approach of the High Court in dealing with the evidence was patently illegal leading to grave miscarriage of justice; The Food Inspector Rep., By The Pp vs Meda Bapu Reddy on 1 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/148970869/ 2 iv) The High Court's judgment is manifestly unjust and unreasonable based on erroneous law and facts on the record of the case; v) This Court must always give proper weight and consideration to the findings of the High Court; vi) This Court would be extremely reluctant in interfering with a case when both the Sessions Court and the High Court have recorded an order of acquittal."
